sections.html:
Towns County lies in the north Georgia mountains against the North Carolina border. Hiawassee is the seat and Young Harris the biggest city. Lake Chatuge fills the northeast corner, and the Chattahoochee National Forest covers part of the county, so many parcels have mountain or lake views.

The population is older, values run high, and owners dominate: 82.3% owner occupancy for 2020-2024 and a typical home value of $316,100. Headcount is up 6.4% over the 2020 base, and 41.2% of residents are past 65. The 2020 count found 8,600 housing units with 36.4% vacant, and some of those may be seasonal or second homes. A person who inherits a mountain cabin from afar should make sure the tax statement is forwarded to a current address.

Statements and payments go through the tax commissioner in the courthouse annex, 48 River Street, Suite H, Hiawassee, GA 30546, phone (706) 896-2267. Weekday service runs from 8:30 until 4:30, with a lunch closure between noon and 1.

The assessor is down the hall in Suite G, reachable at (706) 896-3984 on the same weekday schedule. Parcel records appear on qPublic, which is free. You can also pay online through the county tax website.

  • Commissioner: statements, payments, levies, mobile home tax
  • Assessor: valuations, returns, homestead and conservation forms, mobile home registration
  • Superior court clerk: deeds, with copies handled in the deed room

Rates come from the county Board of Commissioners and the Board of Education, and the commissioner's office has no input.

January 10 is the real estate due date here, which falls later than the usual Georgia schedule. For a check in the mail, a post office postmark counts, and a postage-meter mark does not.

After the date passes, a monthly interest charge posts on the 10th, calculated as the prime rate plus 3 points spread over 12 months. A 5% penalty follows at 120 days, repeating each 120 days until the total reaches 20%. Mobile home bills generally go out about January 2, payable by April 1, with 10% added on April 2.

  • Real estate: due January 10
  • Interest: posted on the 10th of each month
  • Penalty: 5% every 120 days until it reaches 20%
  • Mobile homes: April 1 deadline, 10% penalty the next day

Twelve months of nonpayment sends an account to a collection agency, with administration and levy fees of up to $215 and more, followed by four weeks of newspaper notices ahead of any sale. Pay or arrange terms well before that point.

An owner files an initial return for taxable real and personal property held on January 1, and real estate returns for changed or newly acquired property are due at the assessor's office from January 1 through April 1. After the first real estate return, the law renews it automatically at the prior year's value unless the owner adds land, builds, or otherwise changes the property.

Personal property differs: returns on form PT-50p are filed every year, whatever happened to value or use. An owner who no longer holds the listed items needs to tell the assessor, or the tax keeps coming. Skipping a required return carries a 10% penalty on the unreported value, plus interest and possibly more penalties.

  • New or changed real estate: file by April 1
  • Personal property: file every year
  • Missed return: 10% of the unreported value, plus interest

An owner unhappy with the current value can file a new return stating a different one. If the assessors reject it, that filing starts the appeal described below.

Two programs can follow a parcel into a sale. Tax deferral is open to owners age 62 or older whose gross household income is $15,000 or less. It postpones the bill rather than wiping it out, and the deferred amount generally comes due at a change of ownership or once it reaches 85% of fair market value.

Conservation use is the other. Farm or timber land that qualifies is valued by its current use, and in return the owner signs a 10-year covenant with the assessors. A purchaser who continues the same use and signs the covenant owes no penalty, while a change of use triggers one. Acreage in the hills may already be under a covenant, so check before listing.

Call the assessor at (706) 896-3984, ask whether either program applies to your parcel, and request the terms in writing. A cash buyer taking the home in its present condition will ask for the same figures before closing.

File a homestead application at the Towns County Tax Assessor's Office, and bring a copy of the warranty deed if you are a first-time homeowner. Anything received after April 1 counts toward the next year.

Ownership and residence on January 1 are required. An approved exemption renews itself, though a move, a transfer of title or a switch to another type means applying again. Local exemptions replace the state amounts when the local figure is bigger, so get the current amounts from the assessor rather than an old chart.

Nothing carries over to a buyer. The next bill, now in the buyer's name, can run higher until the new owner files.

Take the appeal to the assessors in writing, counting 45 days from the day the assessment notice was mailed. The grounds are taxability, value, and uniformity with similar properties. Disagreement over the amount of tax levied does not qualify.

When the assessors leave the value alone, the case moves to the equalization board, and Superior Court is the next stop. Arbitration can stand in for the equalization hearing. For an owner away on military duty, a relative or friend may file inside 90 days of the notice.

Mobile homes use a separate track, with 45 days to file with the assessors and 21 days after a change notice to reach the equalization board.

Ask the commissioner for a written balance on every open year, mobile home accounts included, before you accept an offer. Check the superior court clerk's records for any recorded lien, since a title company will want it released before funds move.

The closing agent normally pays those balances out of your proceeds. If the cabin has sat empty, mail may have piled up unread, so ask for the full account history rather than just the latest bill. A cash buyer can take a house that carries tax debt as it stands and clear the balance at the table.

faqs.q: When must Towns County real estate tax be paid?
faqs.a: January 10 every year, with mobile home tax due April 1. A mailed check needs a post office postmark, because a postage-meter mark is not accepted.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Towns County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: Call (706) 896-2267 or visit 48 River Street, Suite H, Hiawassee. Staff are in Monday to Friday, 8:30 until 4:30, and step out for lunch at noon for an hour.

faqs.q: What does late payment cost in Towns County?
faqs.a: Monthly interest posts on the 10th using the prime rate plus 3 points. A 5% penalty arrives at 120 days and returns every 120 days until it hits 20%. Mobile homes pick up a 10% penalty on April 2.

faqs.q: How long can I take to contest a Towns County value?
faqs.a: The window is 45 days counted from the notice's mailing date. Send it to the assessors at (706) 896-3984, and an unsettled appeal moves on to the equalization board.

faqs.q: Will the buyer inherit my Towns County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. It renews each year for the same owner, and a change of ownership calls for a fresh application. The buyer files with the assessor's office by April 1.
